Jess's own surname is a portmanteau, blending her maiden name Farris with her Greek husband's surname Zafiris.
Jess's married surname, made by mashing two surnames together rather than hyphenating them, as an example of portmanteauization.
German word for number, directly related to tally.
An arch servant character of commedia dell'arte, prone to playing tricks, whose name gave English zany.
A recurring commedia dell'arte servant clown, a Venetian form of Gianni, pet form of Giovanni; it gave zany.
From Zanni: someone was first called a zany, a tricky servant type, before the word came to mean a quirky character.
From Zanni, the servant clown of commedia dell'arte; a noun before it was an adjective.
Not used for zapping until Buck Rogers in the 25th Century illustrated it as onomatopoeia; popularised as a ray-gun sound in sci-fi comics, now a verb.
Typeface named after Hermann Zapf's typographical ornaments, called dingbats.
The verlan form of bizarre.
Z in the RAF and Able Baker alphabets, replaced by Zulu because it is pronounced differently in different places.
Honours etymology, coming from Greek zeta through French; Danny says both zed and zee are correct and the rivalry is very modern.
Rhymes with other letter names and suits the alphabet song; Roman letter-naming logic for a fricative would instead favour "ez", matching "ess".
German word cited as related to tide.
A German borrowing meaning time spirit, with the same geist as poltergeist.
An era's intellectual or cultural climate; coined by Johann Gottfried Herder in the 1760s, brought into English by Thomas Carlyle; Zeit is cognate with tide.
Fear of the great mole rat; the hosts don't know why it exists.
Founder of stoicism, who lectured on a painted porch; the philosophy may not bear his name because followers thought him flawed.
Named after Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who supposedly perfected the airship; short for German Zeppelin-Luftschiff.
Named after Ferdinand von Zeppelin.
The original German name for the airship, which Zeppelin.
Prefix for 10^-21, the small counterpart of zetta.
From Arabic sifr, zero or empty, via Latin zephirum; positional systems of the Babylonians, Maya and Gupta India gave it its senses; Romans lacked it.
From the same Arabic source, sifr, as cipher; both share the idea of emptiness, as a ciphered message looks like there is nothing there.
Concept borrowed from Arabic mathematicians; the word comes from Arabic sifr, empty, through several European languages, and shares that origin with cipher.
The Greek letter, which the hosts note is not the source of zetta.
Prefix for 10^21 accepted in the 1990s, a deliberate distortion of Latin septem, with Z avoiding confusion with S for seconds; unrelated to Greek zeta.
A thousand exabytes, using the prefix zetta.
One word governing several parts differently, as in she broke his car and his heart, or Pope's Rape of the Lock; from a root meaning to yoke.
Supposedly used Echo to distract Hera while he chased other nymphs.
The Chinese name for China, meaning middle kingdom.
Shona for houses of stone, a restored indigenous name that replaced Rhodesia.
Named after Johann Gottfried Zinn.
The British word for a zipper.
Originally a trademark; Rob would call his trouser zip his fly, though zipper suits the technology better.
Branded in the US and so more common there than zip; one of the few transatlantic differences in a modern invention's name.
An example of trademark death, a brand name turned generic word.
A genericized trademark, used in a Xerox ad warning that misusing its name could leave its trademark wide open.
From Greek zodiakos kyklos, circle of little animals, though signs like Libra aren't animals; once called the twelve signs, bestiary or Our Lady's way.
From Greek zodiakos kyklos, 'circle of little animals', related to zoology and zoo.
Contains the same Greek word for animal as protozoan.
The spinning device usually showing a galloping horse; its name also derives from a word meaning movement.
An early spinning moving-picture device, often showing a galloping horse; the name meant movement spin, related to tropics.
A common British term for drunk from the linguists' list.
Berlin's western station, Bahnhof Zoo, is named for the zoo; in German, Zoo is pronounced with a ts sound.
Related to zodiac.
Contains the same Greek word for animal as protozoan.
Commenters argue over pronouncing it zoo-ology or zo-ology; Jess switches between them, and Rob sticks with zo-ology.
Related to zodiac.
An Italian word that entered English in America for the long green squash the British call courgettes.
Current Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet, replacing Zebra.
German for twice, literally two times, built on Mal.
The Russian letter like a backwards N, with an ee sound; it descends from Greek eta, so shares its origin with English H.
